learning_experiences: brainstorm the four cardinal points of a compass,
draw and label the four cardinal points, practise giving directions to places using the four cardinal points,
use the four compass points to show direction on the interactive map to enrich the mapping skills.
play computer games on the compass direction for enjoyment.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we show direction of places?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: Learners interact with digital devices as they play computer games on compass direction for enjoyment.
Learning to learn: Learners develop relationships as they share resources and practise giving direction of places using the four cardinal points.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: Learners cooperate as they practise giving direction of places using the four cardinal points.
Respect: Learners show patience as they play computer games on compass direction for enjoyment.
sub_strands.pcis: Creative Thinking: Learners participate in creative games as they play computer games on compass direction for enjoyment.
sub_strands.links: Learners use Creative Arts skills as they draw and label the four cardinal points.

outcomes.text: identify the four cardinal points of a compass
use the four cardinal points to give directions on a map
appreciate the use of four cardinal points in everyday life

skills.name: Name the four cardinal points, their order and their opposites
skills.mastery: The child names north, east, south and west in order round a compass, knows north is opposite south and east is opposite west, knows that facing north east is on the right hand and west on the left, and knows the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the point opposite another
say which side east or west is when facing north
say where the sun rises and sets
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Watching where the sun is in the morning and evening (Grade 1) is how the child finds east and west. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.
North, east, south and west are each a quarter turn apart; the child needs quarter and half turns. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

skills.name: Give directions between places on a described map
skills.mastery: Given a map described in words or a small table, the child says the direction from one place to another, reverses it correctly and gives the direction a walker faces after a quarter turn. Map questions are in words or a small described table, and any county named on a map is an imaginary one. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which direction one place lies from another
turn a direction round (A is north of B, so B is south of A)
say the direction after a turn
read a small table of places

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Naming features between home and school (Grade 1) is the first map of real places the child gives directions on. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong opposite (thinks the opposite of north is east or west).

example.question: Which point is opposite north on a compass?
example.correct_answer: South

misconceptions.cause: The child reads the four points as a list, not as two straight lines crossing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "East" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a plus sign: north at the top, south at the bottom, east and west across. Ask for the point straight across.
misconceptions.feedback: North and south are opposite, and east and west are opposite. The opposite point is straight across the compass.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Swaps east and west (thinks that facing north, east is on the left).

example.question: You face north. Which side is east on?
example.correct_answer: The right hand

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures the compass on a page instead of standing in it.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The left hand" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Have the child stand and face north, stretch out the right arm and say "east". Then turn and do it again.
misconceptions.feedback: Face north and east is on your right hand. West is on your left hand.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, or rises in the north.

example.question: In which direction does the sun rise?
example.correct_answer: The east

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers the sun being high or low but not the side.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The west" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Watch the sun rise on a school morning and name the side; use it to find east and then the other points.
misconceptions.feedback: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the direction the wrong way round (school is north of the market, so says the market is north of the school).

example.question: A school is north of a market. In which direction is the market from the school?
example.correct_answer: South

misconceptions.cause: The child repeats the word in the sentence and does not turn round to the other place.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "North" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Put two objects on the desk. Ask "from this one to that one", then swap and ask again.
misconceptions.feedback: If the school is north of the market, then the market is south of the school. Turn the direction round.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gets the direction wrong after a turn (facing east and turning left gives south).

example.question: Wanjiku faces east and turns left. Which direction does she face now?
example.correct_answer: North

misconceptions.cause: The child turns the wrong way or does not picture facing the direction.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "South" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Have the child stand and face a wall called east, then turn a quarter turn left and name the new wall.
misconceptions.feedback: Facing east, a turn to the left faces north. A turn to the right would face south.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks north means "up" in the sky or uphill, so points at the ceiling or up a slope when asked to face north.

example.question: Stand up and face north. Where do you point?
example.correct_answer: Along the ground, to the left of the morning sun

misconceptions.cause: Maps hang on the wall with north at the top, so the child reads "top of the map" as "up".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Up at the sky" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Lay the map flat on the desk, then on the floor, and turn it so north on the map points along the ground to north.
misconceptions.feedback: North is a direction along the ground, not up. On a flat map it is at the top.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reads "north" as the top of whatever is drawn, even when the map shows a north arrow pointing another way.

example.question: On a map the north arrow points to the right. The well is on the right of the school. Where is the well from the school?
example.wrong_answer: East, because the right is east
example.correct_answer: North, because the arrow shows north is on the right

misconceptions.cause: Most maps in class have north at the top, so the child never looks at the arrow.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "East, because the right is east" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw the same village twice, once with the arrow up and once with the arrow to the right, and ask each time where north is.
misconceptions.feedback: Always look at the north arrow first. North is where the arrow points.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says "left" means west whichever way the person faces.

example.question: Achieng faces south. She turns her head to her left. Which direction is she looking?
example.correct_answer: East

misconceptions.cause: The child learnt "facing north, west is on the left" and uses it for every way of facing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "West" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stand facing south with the class and point: the left hand now points east. Turn and do it for each direction.
misconceptions.feedback: Left and right change when you turn. Compass points stay where they are.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.sub_strand: Location and size of the County
learning_experiences: brainstorm and list sub-counties in their county,
use relevant print or digital resources to identify the location of the county in relation to neighbouring counties,
discuss the size of the county in relation to the neighbouring counties,
sketch, colour, and display the map of the county in class,
play games on the location of the county in relation to neighbouring counties.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to learn the size and location of a county?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: Learners develop simple games as they play games on the location of the county in relation to the neighbouring counties
Learning to learn: Learners search for the location and size of their county
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: Learners engage in assigned roles and duties as they discuss the size of the county in relation to the neighbouring counties
sub_strands.pcis:
Problem Solving: Learners play creative games as they locate the county in relation to the neigbouring counties
Effective Communication: Learners brainstorm to identify sub-counties in their county.
sub_strands.links: English: Learners apply listening and speaking skills as they discuss in groups the size of the county in relation to the neigbouring counties

outcomes.text: identify sub-counties in the county
locate the county in relation to neighbouring counties
estimate the size of the county in relation to neighbouring counties
acknowledge the location and size of the county

skills.name: Say what sub-counties are and how they fit inside the county
skills.mastery: The child knows a county is divided into sub-counties and a sub-county into wards, that a sub-county is smaller than its county, and that a neighbouring county is a different county and not one of its sub-counties. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the unit that is part of a county
put county, sub-county and ward in order of size
say whether a place is inside or outside the county
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Knowing the community around home (Grade 3) is the smallest piece the child fits inside a ward and a sub-county. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.
Locating the local market (Grade 2) is the child's first sense that places sit inside a bigger area. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

skills.name: Locate the county in relation to its neighbouring counties
skills.mastery: Given a described map or table, the child says which neighbouring county lies in each direction, turns the direction round, and names only the counties that share a boundary, not those further away. Map questions are in words or a small described table, and any county named on a map is an imaginary one. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which direction a neighbour lies from the county
name the neighbour in a given direction
say which counties share a boundary
read a small table of neighbours

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Using features on the way to the market (Grade 2) is the first time the child says where one place is from another. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

skills.name: Compare the size of the county with its neighbours
skills.mastery: Given the areas of counties in square kilometres, the child says which is larger and about how many times, compares the whole numbers by their size and not by their first digit, and does not mix up the size of a county with the number of people in it. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which county is larger from the areas given
say about how many times larger one is
tell size from population
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Comparing county areas means ordering whole numbers by their size, not their first digit. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a sub-county is bigger than a county.

example.question: Which is bigger, a county or a sub-county?
example.correct_answer: A county

misconceptions.cause: The child knows both names and not which holds the other.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A sub-county" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Use boxes inside boxes: the county box holds several sub-county boxes, which hold wards.
misconceptions.feedback: A county is divided into sub-counties. Many sub-counties make one county, so the county is bigger.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts county, sub-county and ward in the wrong order of size.

example.question: Which is the smallest unit: county, sub-county or ward?
example.correct_answer: Ward

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard the three words but not learned how they nest.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sub-county" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw the three nested boxes and label them from the outside in; then ask for smallest and largest.
misconceptions.feedback: A county is the biggest. It has sub-counties, and each sub-county has wards. A ward is the smallest.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a neighbouring county is a sub-county of the learner's own county.

example.question: Kalia County has a neighbour called Mwangaza County. Is Mwangaza one of the sub-counties of Kalia?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a sub-county of Kalia
example.correct_answer: No, it is a separate county next to Kalia

misconceptions.cause: The child treats everything nearby as inside the home county.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it is a sub-county of Kalia" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw two county boxes side by side and a boundary line between them; sub-counties are drawn inside one box only.
misconceptions.feedback: A neighbouring county is a different county. Sub-counties are only the parts inside one county.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reverses the direction of a neighbour.

example.question: On a map, Kitale County lies north of Meru County. In which direction is Meru County from Kitale County?
example.correct_answer: South

misconceptions.cause: The child repeats the word in the sentence and does not turn round.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "North" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Mark two dots on paper and ask the direction from each dot to the other.
misconceptions.feedback: If Kitale lies north of Meru, then Meru lies south of Kitale.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a county a neighbour when it does not share a boundary with the county.

example.question: Which county is a neighbour of Kalia County, with a shared boundary?
example.correct_answer: The county whose boundary touches Kalia

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks near means next to.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A county two counties away" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Use a described map: trace the boundary of the county and name only the counties that touch it.
misconceptions.feedback: A neighbour shares a boundary with the county. A county with another county between is not a neighbour.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the county with more people is the bigger county.

example.question: County A has 3,000 square kilometres and 900,000 people. County B has 12,000 square kilometres and 400,000 people. Which county is larger in size?
example.wrong_answer: County A, because it has more people
example.correct_answer: County B, because its area is larger

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up how big a place is with how many people live there.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "County A, because it has more people" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a large empty field and a small crowded classroom: which has more space and which has more people?
misconceptions.feedback: Size is the area of the land in square kilometres. The number of people tells how crowded it is, not how big it is.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Compares numbers by their first digit instead of their size (thinks 800 is more than 3,000 because 8 is more than 3).

example.question: County A is 800 square kilometres and County B is 3,000 square kilometres. Which is larger?
example.correct_answer: County B

misconceptions.cause: The child looks at the first digit and not at the number of digits.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "County A" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write the two numbers in a place value table and compare the thousands first.
misconceptions.feedback: Compare the whole numbers. 3,000 is more than 800, so County B has the larger area.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the ward is the same as the county because both elect someone (an MCA and a Governor).

example.question: Which is smaller: a ward or a county?
example.correct_answer: A ward; many wards make a sub-county and many sub-counties make a county

misconceptions.cause: The child links each area to a leader and sees two leaders as two equal places.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They are the same size" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Fit the puzzle: wards into a sub-county, sub-counties into the county, and count the pieces.
misconceptions.feedback: A county holds sub-counties, and each sub-county holds wards. A ward is the smallest.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a town inside the county is a neighbouring county.

example.question: Kibo Town is inside Mlima County. Is Kibo Town a neighbour county of Mlima?
example.correct_answer: No, it is inside Mlima County, not beside it

misconceptions.cause: The child uses "near" as the test of a neighbour, and a town inside is very near.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it is close by" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: On the cut-out map, put a dot for the town inside the county and colour the counties that share the edge.
misconceptions.feedback: A neighbour county is outside your county and shares its boundary.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a county can have only one neighbour in each direction.

example.question: Two counties both lie to the north of Mlima County and touch it. How many northern neighbours does Mlima have?
example.wrong_answer: One; only one county can be north
example.correct_answer: Two

misconceptions.cause: Simple maps in class show one neighbour on each side, like a cross.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "One; only one county can be north" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a county with two counties along its northern edge and count them.
misconceptions.feedback: A county can have more than one neighbour on the same side.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Judges size by how big a county looks on two maps of different scales.

example.question: Map A shows Ziwa County large on a full page. Map B shows Mlima County small in a corner. The table says Ziwa is 2,000 square kilometres and Mlima 6,000. Which is bigger?
example.correct_answer: Mlima, 6,000 is more than 2,000 square kilometres

misconceptions.cause: The child trusts the picture and does not know two maps can be drawn to different sizes.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Ziwa, it looks bigger" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw the same classroom on a big sheet and on a small card: the room did not change size.
misconceptions.feedback: Use the numbers in square kilometres, not how big a picture looks.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Compares the numbers and ignores the units, so 3 thousand square kilometres looks smaller than 900.

example.question: Ziwa County is 3 thousand square kilometres. Mlima is 900 square kilometres. Which is bigger?
example.correct_answer: Ziwa, 3 thousand is 3,000, which is more than 900

misconceptions.cause: The child reads the digit and skips the word "thousand".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mlima, 900 is more than 3" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write both as full numbers, 3,000 and 900, and line up the digits by place value.
misconceptions.feedback: Read the whole number with its word. 3 thousand is 3,000.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: brainstorm the main physical features in the county, sketch the main physical features in the county,
draw or take photographs of the main physical features in the county,
outline the importance of the main physical features in the county and share the discussion points in class,
display pictures or models of the main physical features in the county in class,
find out from parents or guardians the main physical features in the county and share.
key_inquiry_questions: Which physical features are found in your county?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Citizenship: Learners identify the main physical features in their county.
Learning to: Learners find out from parents or guardians the physical features in the county and share
sub_strands.values: Social Justice: Learners accord equal opportunities in sharing responsibilities as they outline the importance of the main physical features in the county and share the discussion points in class.
sub_strands.pcis: Self-Awareness: Learners appreciate each other’s abilities as they draw some of the main physical features in the county.
sub_strands.links: English: Learners use speaking skills as they discuss in groups the importance of the main physical features in the county in class.

outcomes.text: identify the main physical features in the county
state the importance of the main physical features in the county
illustrate the main physical features in the county
appreciate the main physical features in the county

skills.name: Identify the main kinds of physical feature in a county
skills.mastery: The child names a hill (low rounded high ground), a mountain (much higher), a valley (low land between hills or mountains), a plain (wide flat land), a river (water flowing in a channel), a lake (water with land around it) and the ocean coast from a short description. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the kind of feature from a description
pick the odd one out
tell a hill from a mountain, a river from a lake, a plain from a valley
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Grade 1 named the features between home and school; Grade 4 sorts them into kinds. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.
Naming features on the way to market (Grade 2) gives the child real hills and rivers to sort. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

skills.name: State how physical features help people
skills.mastery: The child matches rivers and lakes to water, fish and irrigation, mountains and hills to rain, forests and tourism, plains to farming and building, and the coast to fishing and ports, and does not call a feature useless or give it a use it does not have. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: match a feature to its use
say why a feature matters to the people near it
pick the false use
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Knowing sources of water (Grade 1) is the root of "rivers and lakes give water". Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a hill and a mountain are the same or a hill is higher.

example.question: Which is higher, a hill or a mountain?
example.correct_answer: A mountain

misconceptions.cause: The child uses the two words for any raised ground.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A hill" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare Mount Kenya with a small hill near school: describe the height of each.
misconceptions.feedback: A mountain is much higher than a hill. A hill is lower and usually rounded.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up a river and a lake.

example.question: Which one is water that flows along in a channel?
example.correct_answer: A river

misconceptions.cause: The child knows both have water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A lake" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: does the water stay in one place or move on to the sea or a lake?
misconceptions.feedback: A river flows along a channel. A lake is water that stays in a hollow, with land all round it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up a plain and a valley (thinks a valley is wide flat land).

example.question: Which is wide flat land?
example.correct_answer: A plain

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks low land is flat land.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A valley" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a bowl and a flat table: a valley lies between high land on both sides, a plain is wide and flat.
misconceptions.feedback: A plain is wide, flat land. A valley is low land between hills or mountains.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks physical features have no use for people (only beautiful).

example.question: Why is a river important to people near it?
example.wrong_answer: It is only nice to look at
example.correct_answer: It gives water for drinking, farming and fish

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the features as scenery.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is only nice to look at" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask each learner to name one thing in the day that comes from water or land near home.
misconceptions.feedback: Physical features are useful. Rivers give water and fish, mountains bring rain and visitors, plains give farmland.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Matches a feature to a use it does not have (farming on a lake, fishing on a plain).

example.question: Which feature is best for fishing?
example.correct_answer: A lake

misconceptions.cause: The child guesses from the word and not from what the feature is.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A plain" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Match each feature to what it is made of: water, high ground, flat land. Then ask what each can give.
misconceptions.feedback: Fish live in water, so lakes, rivers and the sea give fish. Plains are flat dry land, good for farming.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks mountains and valleys only get in the way and do no good.

example.question: How does a mountain help people?
example.correct_answer: It brings rain, rivers and visitors

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the difficulty of travelling over a mountain.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It only blocks the road" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Trace a river from its source on a mountain to the farms below.
misconceptions.feedback: Mountains help us. Rain falls on them and feeds rivers, they grow tea and trees, and visitors come to climb them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Counts a dam, a road or a building as a physical feature.

example.question: Which of these is a physical feature: a hill, a road, a school?
example.correct_answer: A hill

misconceptions.cause: The child takes "physical" to mean anything you can see and touch.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A road" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sort pictures into "made by nature" and "made by people": only nature's go in the physical features box.
misconceptions.feedback: Physical features are made by nature: hills, rivers, lakes, valleys. Roads and buildings are made by people.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a swamp or wetland is only a dirty, useless place to be drained.

example.question: What is a swamp good for?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing; it should be filled in
example.correct_answer: It holds water, gives papyrus and reeds and is home to fish and birds

misconceptions.cause: The child knows swamps as muddy places with mosquitoes and has never seen what they give.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing; it should be filled in" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show papyrus mats or baskets and ask where the papyrus grows.
misconceptions.feedback: Swamps store water, give reeds for mats and baskets and are homes for birds and fish.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

say what a farmer does in a season
say what people wear or sell in a season

skills.mastery: The child says rain makes roads slippery, muddy and sometimes flooded and makes it harder to see, that a driver must slow down, and that a person must never cross flooded water, never run across a road, and wait in a safe place. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say what rain does to a road
choose the safe thing to do near a flooded road
say what a driver should do in heavy rain
find the false step in a learner's answer

Grade 3 Environmental Activities taught the idea first. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
The dangers of bad weather (Grade 3) lead straight into rain on roads. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses spring, summer, autumn and winter as the seasons of the county.

example.question: Which of these is a season in our county?
example.correct_answer: The rainy season

misconceptions.cause: The child has met the four names in picture books from other lands.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Autumn" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask the child to name the weather of each month of the school year, then give each stretch its own name.
misconceptions.feedback: Our seasons are hot, cold, dry and rainy. Autumn and winter belong to places far from the equator.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the seasons (thinks the rainy season is the hot season, or cold means rain).

example.question: When there is little rain and no clouds for many days, which season is it?
example.correct_answer: The dry season

misconceptions.cause: The child names a season by one feature and not by the whole.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The rainy season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make a weather chart over a week and name the season from what it shows.
misconceptions.feedback: No rain for many days is the dry season. Long rains come about March to May and short rains about October to December.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Treats one day of weather as a whole season.

example.question: It rained on Tuesday. What can we say?
example.wrong_answer: It is now the rainy season
example.correct_answer: It rained that day, and a season lasts for many weeks

misconceptions.cause: The child does not tell weather of a day from a season.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is now the rainy season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the weather was every day of one month, then name the season.
misconceptions.feedback: One rainy day is weather. A season is the weather that comes for many weeks, month after month.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks farmers should plant when the ground is dry.

example.question: When do farmers plant maize?
example.correct_answer: When the rains begin

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link the seeds to the need for water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the dry season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Plant two cups of beans, water one, and compare after a week.
misconceptions.feedback: Farmers plant when the rains begin, so that the seeds get water. They harvest and dry the crop in the dry season.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Matches a season to an activity that does not fit it (warm sweaters in the hot season).

example.question: What do people wear in the cold season?
example.correct_answer: Warm clothes such as sweaters

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think of the weather of the season.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Light cotton shirts only" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the child wears on a cold morning and what on a hot afternoon.
misconceptions.feedback: In the cold season people wear sweaters and jackets. In the hot season they wear light clothes.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks seasons make no difference to what people do.

example.question: Do seasons change what people do?
example.wrong_answer: No, people do the same all year
example.correct_answer: Yes, farmers, traders and travellers change what they do

misconceptions.cause: The child lives in a town and does not see farming.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, people do the same all year" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what changes at home when the rains start: crops, roads, clothes, school trips.
misconceptions.feedback: Seasons change many things: when farmers plant and harvest, what people wear, sell and how they travel.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it is safe to run across a wet road to get out of the rain.

example.question: It is raining. What should Njeri do at the road?
example.wrong_answer: Run across fast to get out of the rain
example.correct_answer: Wait at the side and cross only when the road is clear

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of being dry, not of slippery roads and poor sight.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Run across fast to get out of the rain" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play crossing in the rain: slow, look both ways, hold a friend's hand.
misconceptions.feedback: Never run across a road. Rain makes roads slippery and drivers cannot see well. Wait and cross when it is clear.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it is safe to cross flooded water if it looks shallow.

example.question: A road has water flowing across it after heavy rain. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: Cross if the water looks shallow
example.correct_answer: Do not cross: go back and tell an adult

misconceptions.cause: The child cannot judge how deep or how fast water is.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cross if the water looks shallow" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a picture of a drift in flood; ask what is hidden under the water.
misconceptions.feedback: Never cross flooded water. It may be deep, strong and hide holes. Wait or find another way with an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks rain makes the road safer or that drivers should speed up to get out of the rain.

example.question: How should a driver drive in heavy rain?
example.wrong_answer: Faster, to get out of the rain
example.correct_answer: Slowly, because the road is slippery and it is hard to see

misconceptions.cause: The child links getting home sooner with safety.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Faster, to get out of the rain" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask how long it takes to stop on a slippery floor when you run.
misconceptions.feedback: Rain makes roads slippery, so a vehicle takes longer to stop. A driver must go slowly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every county has its rains in the same months and the same seasons as their own.

example.question: Is the rainy season in the same months in every part of Kenya?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it rains at the same time everywhere
example.correct_answer: No, the months of the rains differ from place to place

misconceptions.cause: The child has only lived through one county's calendar.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it rains at the same time everywhere" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare the class chart with a chart from another region read out by the teacher.
misconceptions.feedback: Seasons come at different times in different parts of Kenya.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks crops are harvested and dried in the rainy season.

example.question: When do farmers dry and store their maize?
example.correct_answer: In the dry season

misconceptions.cause: The child knows rain makes crops grow and links rain with the whole farming year.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the rainy season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what happens to maize left out to dry in the rain: it rots.
misconceptions.feedback: Farmers plant when the rains start and dry their harvest in the dry season.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks holding an umbrella or wearing dark clothes in heavy rain makes a walker easy for drivers to see.

example.question: It is raining heavily in the evening. What helps drivers see a walker?
example.wrong_answer: Dark clothes and an umbrella over the face
example.correct_answer: Bright or reflective clothes and walking facing the traffic

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks only about keeping dry, not about being seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Dark clothes and an umbrella over the face" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: In a dim room, hold up a dark cloth and a bright one: which do you see first?
misconceptions.feedback: In rain, wear bright clothes and walk facing the traffic so drivers see you.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify museums, monuments and cultural centres
skills.mastery: The child says a museum keeps and shows old objects and records, a monument is a structure built to remember a person or event, and a cultural centre shows the way of life of communities, and knows a place is historic because of its age and meaning, not because it is new or big. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the kind of place from its job
pick the place that is a historic built environment
pick the odd one out
find the false step in a learner's answer

Naming the features between home and school (Grade 1), buildings among them, is the first look at places people built. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

skills.name: Explain why historic built environments matter
skills.mastery: The child says historic places teach history, keep a community's identity, bring visitors and need to be cared for, and does not say they should be pulled down because they are old. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the reason a place is kept
say what people gain from visiting
say how to treat a historic place
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Sorting events by how they help a community (Grade 3) is the same thinking applied to places. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up a museum and a monument.

example.question: Which place keeps and shows old objects and records?
example.correct_answer: A museum

misconceptions.cause: The child treats all old built places as the same thing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A monument" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: where do you go inside to see old tools and pictures, and what do you pass in a town square that remembers a person?
misconceptions.feedback: A museum keeps and shows old objects. A monument is a structure built to remember a person or an event.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any big or famous new building is a historic built environment.

example.question: Which is a historic built environment?
example.correct_answer: An old fort that still stands

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks big or famous means historic.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A new shopping mall" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask for the date of each place and what it tells about the past.
misconceptions.feedback: A historic place is old and tells about the past. A new mall is not historic, however big it is.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a cultural centre is a market or a shop.

example.question: What is a cultural centre?
example.wrong_answer: A place to buy and sell goods
example.correct_answer: A place that shows the way of life of communities

misconceptions.cause: The child links "centre" with a shopping centre.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A place to buy and sell goods" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what you might see and do at a cultural centre: dances, houses, crafts, food.
misconceptions.feedback: A cultural centre shows the traditions of communities, such as dance, food, dress and crafts.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks old places should be pulled down because they are old.

example.question: An old fort is crumbling. What should the county do?
example.wrong_answer: Pull it down and build a new shop
example.correct_answer: Repair and protect it because it tells our history

misconceptions.cause: The child values only what is new.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Pull it down and build a new shop" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a grandmother's stories give that a new book does not, then link this to old places.
misconceptions.feedback: Historic places cannot be rebuilt once they are gone. They teach history and keep our identity, so we protect them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks historic places matter only for the money from visitors.

example.question: Why do we keep museums and monuments?
example.wrong_answer: Only to earn money from visitors
example.correct_answer: To learn about the past and keep our identity, and visitors also bring income

misconceptions.cause: The child sees one reason where there are several.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only to earn money from visitors" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Brainstorm three reasons for keeping a place; mark which are about learning and which about income.
misconceptions.feedback: Visitors bring income, but the first reasons are learning about the past and keeping the identity of the community.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks ruins are broken rubbish and not a historic site because the buildings are not whole.

example.question: Gede has old broken walls with no roofs. Is it a historic built environment?
example.wrong_answer: No, it is only broken stones
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is ruins of an old town that tell us how people lived

misconceptions.cause: The child judges a place by whether it looks good now.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it is only broken stones" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a photo of Gede and a drawing of what the town looked like; ask what the walls tell us.
misconceptions.feedback: Ruins are old buildings left from long ago. They tell us how people lived.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks historic places are only for foreign tourists, not for local people.

example.question: Who can learn from a museum in the county?
example.correct_answer: Everyone: learners, families and visitors

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen tourists at such places on television and not local families.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only visitors from other countries" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Plan a class visit or show a photo of a school group in a museum.
misconceptions.feedback: Historic places are for all of us. They teach us our own history.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks writing names on an old wall or taking a stone home shows love for the place.

example.question: Which shows care for a historic site?
example.wrong_answer: Writing your name on the wall to remember the visit
example.correct_answer: Keeping it clean and leaving everything as you found it

misconceptions.cause: The child copies what they have seen visitors do and thinks it is a way of remembering.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Writing your name on the wall to remember the visit" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the wall would look like if every visitor wrote on it.
misconceptions.feedback: We care for old places by keeping them clean and leaving them as we found them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify the ways people depend on each other in a county
skills.mastery: The child names trade (a farmer sells to a shopkeeper), farming (farmers feed others), the hospital (health workers care for the sick) and places of worship (leaders guide people) as ways people depend on each other, and says that each side needs the other. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

say what a worker gives others
match a place or worker to what it gives
find the false step in a learner's answer

Places where family needs are met (Grade 2) show that the family gets its needs from others. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

skills.name: Explain the benefits of people depending on each other
skills.mastery: The child says depending on each other gives us goods and services we cannot make ourselves, brings income, lets people use different skills and builds friendship, and does not say a family can supply every need alone. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the benefit of sharing work
say what happens when nobody depends on anyone
say who gains from a trade
find the false step in a learner's answer

How emotional needs are met by others (Grade 3) is one benefit of depending on each other beyond money. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a family can make or grow everything it needs.

example.question: Can one family grow, make and do everything it needs?
example.correct_answer: No, so people depend on each other

misconceptions.cause: The child sees one family in the home, not the work of others behind each thing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, if it works hard" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List what a family uses in one day and who made each thing.
misconceptions.feedback: No family can do everything. People depend on farmers, traders, health workers and many others.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only one side depends on the other (the shopkeeper does not need the farmer).

example.question: A farmer sells vegetables to a shopkeeper. Who needs the other?
example.wrong_answer: Only the farmer needs the shopkeeper
example.correct_answer: Both need each other

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the farmer as the one with the problem.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only the farmer needs the shopkeeper" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the shopkeeper sells if no farmers sell to him, and what the farmer does if there is no shop.
misconceptions.feedback: Each needs the other. The farmer needs a market, and the shopkeeper needs goods to sell.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Matches a worker or place to the wrong service (a hospital for food, a church for medicine).

example.question: What does a hospital give people?
example.correct_answer: Care for the sick

misconceptions.cause: The child guesses from the building and not from what it does.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Food to eat" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make a matching chart of five places and what they give.
misconceptions.feedback: A hospital gives care for the sick. A farm gives food, and a place of worship gives spiritual guidance.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks needing other people is a weakness or a bad thing.

example.question: Is it bad to depend on other people?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, strong people do things alone
example.correct_answer: No, it lets everyone use their skills and gain more

misconceptions.cause: The child equates depending on others with being unable.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, strong people do things alone" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask who made the school desk, who grew the lunch and who taught the lesson.
misconceptions.feedback: Depending on each other is a strength. We get what we cannot make and share what we can.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the only benefit of trade or sharing is money.

example.question: What do people get when they depend on each other?
example.correct_answer: Goods and services they cannot make and also friendship and income

misconceptions.cause: The child links trade only to cash.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only money" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a neighbour who lends a tool gives that is not money.
misconceptions.feedback: People get goods, services, skills, income and friendship. Money is only one benefit.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a rich person does not depend on anyone because they can pay.

example.question: A rich trader has lots of money. Does she depend on other people?
example.wrong_answer: No, money means she needs nobody
example.correct_answer: Yes, she needs farmers, drivers, doctors and workers

misconceptions.cause: The child sees money as the thing that meets needs, not the people money pays.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, money means she needs nobody" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what she can buy if every farmer and shopkeeper stopped working.
misconceptions.feedback: Money only helps because other people grow, make and sell things. Everyone depends on others.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks people depend on each other only in towns, and village families live alone.

example.question: Do people in a village depend on each other?
example.wrong_answer: No, village families do everything alone
example.correct_answer: Yes, they share work, trade at the market and help at weddings and funerals

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures a village home growing its own food and misses the sharing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, village families do everything alone" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List what a village family gets from others: the posho mill, the market, the clinic, help at harvest.
misconceptions.feedback: In villages and towns, people depend on each other for goods, services and help.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not see that depending on each other creates jobs.

example.question: Farmers need lorries to take milk to the factory. What does this give the lorry driver?
example.correct_answer: A job and an income

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the person who needs help gaining.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, the farmer gains" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Act it out: the farmer pays the driver; who has money now?
misconceptions.feedback: When people depend on each other, both sides gain. The driver gets work and pay.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Describe how people are spread over a county and the reasons
skills.mastery: The child says population distribution is how people are spread over an area, that dense means many people for the space and sparse few, and gives reasons: many people live where soil is fertile, rain is reliable, there is water, work, roads, health care and security, and few where it is very dry, steep, flooded or unsafe. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say whether an area is dense or sparse from the figures
pick the reason an area has many or few people
tell distribution from total population
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Sorting places as safe and unsafe (Grade 3) is one reason people settle in some places and avoid others. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up population distribution with the total number of people.

example.question: What does population distribution mean?
example.wrong_answer: The total number of people in a county
example.correct_answer: How people are spread over an area

misconceptions.cause: The child links "population" with counting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The total number of people in a county" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Place twelve counters on a page: first all in one corner, then spread out; the total is the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Distribution is how people are spread over the area. The total number is a different thing.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a dense area is a large area.

example.question: An area has many people living close together. Is it dense or sparse?
example.correct_answer: Dense

misconceptions.cause: The child links dense with large size or fills the word with a different meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sparse" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare ten learners in a small room and ten on a football pitch.
misconceptions.feedback: Dense means many people in a small space. Sparse means few people spread over a large space.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives reasons the wrong way round (people crowd into very dry, steep or unsafe places).

example.question: Why do many people live near a river with good soil and rain?
example.wrong_answer: Because there is no water there
example.correct_answer: Because they get water, food and work there

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link where people live with what the land gives.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Because there is no water there" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the family needs each day and where they find it.
misconceptions.feedback: People live where they can get water, food, work, roads and safety. Dry, steep, flooded or unsafe places have few people.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks people are spread evenly over a county, the same number on every piece of land.

example.question: Is the number of people the same in every part of a county?
example.correct_answer: No, some parts are crowded and others have few people

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures the county map as one colour.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, people spread out evenly" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Drop beans on the map where the class thinks people live; the beans bunch up.
misconceptions.feedback: People are not spread evenly. Many live where there is water, work and good land.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify the aspects of traditional culture and sort examples into them
skills.mastery: The child names the six aspects of traditional culture (dressing, food, housing, artefacts, sports and games, festivals and ceremonies), sorts everyday examples into them, knows culture is alive and not only the past, and knows communities in one county can have different traditions. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the aspect an item belongs to
match a practice to its aspect
say whether a statement about culture is true
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Grade 3 classified cultural events; Grade 4 sorts the wider aspects of culture. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.
Food, clothing and shelter, the basic needs of Grade 1, are three aspects of traditional culture: traditional food, dressing and housing. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Sorts an example under the wrong aspect (a drum under dressing, ugali under housing).

example.question: Under which aspect of culture is a kiondo (a sisal basket)?
example.correct_answer: Artefacts

misconceptions.cause: The child sorts by the first thing that comes to mind.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Dressing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make six boxes, one for each aspect, and sort a pile of picture cards.
misconceptions.feedback: A kiondo is made by hand, so it is an artefact. Clothes are dressing, ugali is food, a manyatta is housing.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks traditional culture belongs only to the past or only to old people.

example.question: Is traditional culture still practised today?
example.correct_answer: Yes, many people still practise it

misconceptions.cause: The child sees culture as something in a museum.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it is finished" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask which dishes, songs and ceremonies the family still shares.
misconceptions.feedback: Culture is alive. People still practise many traditions, in food, dress, songs, games and ceremonies.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks all communities in a county have the same traditions.

example.question: Do all the communities in a county have the same traditions?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, they all do the same things
example.correct_answer: No, each community has its own as well as shared ones

misconceptions.cause: The child knows only the home community well.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, they all do the same things" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask each learner to name one dish, dance or dress from their own community.
misconceptions.feedback: Communities differ in dress, food, houses and ceremonies, and respecting the differences keeps us at peace.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks traditional culture is backward and should all be dropped.

example.question: A learner says all traditional culture is backward. What is a good reply?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it should all be stopped
example.correct_answer: No: much of it, like songs, food and respect for elders, is still good today

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard harmful customs criticised and puts all culture with them.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it should all be stopped" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List good parts of culture the class still enjoys: food, songs, games, respect for elders.
misconceptions.feedback: Many parts of traditional culture are good and alive today. Only harmful customs should stop.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Explain the values of the school from a situation
skills.mastery: Given a short school situation, the child names the value it shows (respect, honesty, responsibility, hard work, unity, cleanliness) and says why it matters, and does not treat values as the same thing as written rules or punishments. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the value a learner shows
pick the action that shows a value
say why a value matters
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Rights and responsibilities at school (Grade 2) are where the child first meets doing right by others. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.
Keeping the school clean (Grade 2) is the child's lived example of the value of cleanliness and responsibility. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher.

misconceptions.error: Names the wrong value for a situation (calls handing in lost money respect, not honesty).

example.question: Wekesa finds a lost shilling coin and hands it to the teacher. Which value does he show?
example.correct_answer: Honesty

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the words and does not tie them to actions.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Hard work" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make cards of the value words and match them to six short scenes.
misconceptions.feedback: Handing in what is not yours is honesty. Respect is speaking and acting kindly to others.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks values are the same as rules or punishments.

example.question: Which is a value of a school?
example.correct_answer: Respect

misconceptions.cause: The child links school with rules and punishments.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The cane" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask the child what a value is: a good idea that guides us, even without a teacher watching.
misconceptions.feedback: A value is a belief about what is good, such as respect or honesty. Rules and punishments are different.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a value matters only when a teacher is watching.

example.question: Juma picks up litter when no teacher is near. Is he showing a value?
example.correct_answer: Yes, he shows responsibility and cleanliness

misconceptions.cause: The child links values to praise or punishment from a teacher.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, nobody saw it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask whether the compound is cleaner whether or not a teacher saw it.
misconceptions.feedback: A value is what you do because it is right, even when no one is watching.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the school motto is the same as a school value or a rule.

example.question: Our motto is "Strive to excel". Is the motto a school rule?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a rule we are punished for breaking
example.correct_answer: No: a motto is a short saying that guides the school; values are qualities we show

misconceptions.cause: Motto, values and rules are all written on the same notice board.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it is a rule we are punished for breaking" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Read the notice board together and sort: motto, values, rules.
misconceptions.feedback: A motto is a short guiding saying. Values are qualities. Rules say what to do.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Social Studies teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
